paragraphs.source_en: Yet once I had resolved to do something, to give it up halfway felt somehow regrettable, like waiting eagerly for an evening shower only to see the dark clouds pass away into the neighboring district. Besides, if the right were not on our side that would be another matter; but for justice and for humanity, even if it came to nothing and meant throwing away my life, I ought to go through with it. That, surely, is the true spirit of a man who knows what duty is. For me, a cat, a little wasted effort and a little mud on my paws are no more than I should properly accept. Since I was born a cat, I lack the nimble three-inch tongue with which Messrs. Kangetsu, Meitei, and Kushami exchange opinions; but precisely because I am a cat, I surpass those gentlemen in the art of slipping secretly into other people's houses. To accomplish what human beings cannot is, in itself, a very great pleasure. Even if I learn the inside story of Kaneda by fighting alone, that is far more pleasant than nobody knowing it at all. Even if I cannot tell anyone, merely giving them the awareness that their affairs may be spied out by others is enough to comfort me. With these pleasures arising one after another, I could not help but go. Let me, then, take this heavy responsibility upon myself.

paragraphs.source_en: When I went to the alley opposite, there, just as I had heard, a Western-style house was arrogantly occupying a large corner lot. I thought the master of this house must be as haughty as the Western building itself. I entered the gate and inspected the building for a while; apart from giving one a sense of oppressive dignity and having a two-story structure standing there to no purpose, it was a construction without any particular merit. This, I suppose, is what Meitei meant by commonplace. Keeping the front entrance to my right, I passed through the shrubbery and went around to the kitchen door. The kitchen was indeed spacious, certainly ten times the size of Mr. Kushami's kitchen. The utensils were set out in perfect order and shone brilliantly. I daresay it would not be inferior to Count Okuma's kitchen, which was described in detail the other day in the Nippon newspaper. I thought to myself, “Now this is a model kitchen.” So I crept farther inside. When I looked in, the rickshawman's wife was standing in a lime-hardened earthen floor of about twelve feet square, chattering away with the cook-maid and the rickshawman. “This is dangerous,” I thought, and hurriedly hid behind a water bucket. The cook of the house said, “Does that teacher really not know our master's name?” “How could he not know it? Anyone around here who doesn't know Master Kaneda's mansion must be blind with his eyes open!” That was the voice of the private rickshawman. The rickshawman's wife said, “It's hard to say. That teacher is an odd fellow who knows nothing except books. If he knew even a little about the master he might be somewhat afraid, but he knows nothing at all; he doesn't even know the ages of his own children.” The rickshawman said, “You mean even mentioning the Kaneda household won't make him behave? What a troublesome, obstinate blockhead! But never mind. Damn it, why don't we all get together and frighten him a bit?” The rickshawman's wife said, “That would certainly be good. The things they say are simply awful, saying our mistress's nose is absurdly big and that they can't stand the sight of her face. He should look at his own face, just like a ceramic tanuki. Ugly as he is, he thinks he's perfectly presentable. It makes one sick!” The cook said, “It isn't only his face. Isn't the way he carries a towel and goes to the bathhouse unbearably stuck-up too? He probably thinks there is nobody greater than himself.” It seems that Mr. Kushami was highly unpopular even in the eyes of the cook-maid. The rickshawman said, “Let's all go over and stand by that fellow's fence and heap abuse on him. Agreed?” The rickshawman's wife said, “If we do that to him, he'll surely become obedient.” The rickshawman said, “But the mistress just ordered us that it wouldn't do to let him see us. We should let him hear only our voices, stop him from studying, and irritate him as much as possible.” The rickshawman's wife said, “I understand that.” What she meant was that she would take on one third of the job of saying nasty things. I thought, so this lot are the ones who come to torment Mr. Kushami.

paragraphs.source_zh: 我到对面的胡同一看，果然像刚才听说的那样，一座洋房傲然地占据着胡同拐角的一大块地方。我想这家的主人也会和洋房一样的倨傲吧。我走进门去，看了一会这座建筑物，它除了给人一种威严压抑的感觉和二层楼房毫无意义地直立在那里以外，是个没有特色的结构。迷亭所说“平庸”，大概就是指这个吧。我从正门向右，穿过花木园后，转到了厨房门口。厨房倒是真宽大，肯定有苦沙弥先生的厨房的十倍大。用具摆得齐齐整整，精光锃亮。大概不会劣于前些日子在《日本新闻》上详细报道过的大隈伯的厨房吧。我心想：“这可是模范厨房啊。”于是我又往里面走。进去一看，那个车夫的老婆正站在十二尺见方、用石灰拍牢的“土间”里和烧饭的女仆、人力车夫在哇啦哇啦讲着什么呢。“这太危险啦，”我急忙藏到水桶后边。他家烧饭的厨娘说：“那个教员，难道不晓得咱们老爷的名字？”“怎么会不晓得？这一带要是不晓得金田老爷的公馆，那只能是睁眼瞎！”这是专用人力车夫的声音。车夫的老婆说：“很难说呀。那个教师是个怪人，除了书本外什么也不懂。他对老爷哪怕多少知道点也会怕几分的，可他什么也不知道，连他自己孩子的年龄都不晓得哩。”车夫说：“向他提金田家，他还不驯顺吗？真是个难调理的死脑瓜子！不过不要紧。他妈的，咱们大伙儿合起来吓唬他一下好不好？”车夫的老婆说：“那当然好。他们说的话难听死啦，什么咱们太太的鼻子大得出奇啦，什么看着咱们太太的面孔就不顺眼啦。他也不看看自己那副活像陶瓷狸精的面孔哩。别看他是个丑八怪，可他自己却认为蛮过得去呢，真叫人恶心！”烧饭的厨娘说：“不光是那张面孔，他那拎着澡巾上澡堂去的样子，不也自高自大得不得了吗？他可能认为没有比他更了不起的啦。”看来苦沙弥先生连在烧饭女仆的眼中，也是很不得人心的。车夫说道：“咱们大伙儿都去，在那家伙的墙脚下说他的坏话，你们同意吧。”车夫的老婆说：“这样搞他一下，他肯定会老实起来的。”车夫说：“不过刚才太太吩咐下来，要是让他看见了咱们可不太好。只让他能听得见声音，使他无法看书，尽量惹他发火就行。”车夫的老婆说：“这个我知道。”她的意思是在说，她可以把说讨厌话包下三分之一来。我心想，这群家伙要来捉弄苦沙弥先生哩。

paragraphs.source_en: I quietly slipped past the three of them and went inside.
